comment_text.value:
Hi HN, kc is a Kotlin compiler for the JVM, written in Go.

Why I built it: most Kotlin tools, like linters, KSP and the language server, are built on kotlinc's frontend, so they're only as fast as it is. A fast frontend could make room for:

- Linters that run in milliseconds instead of seconds

- A fast language server

- Much faster KSP annotation processing

- Quicker builds in CI, where every run starts a cold JVM

- Fast feedback for coding agents, which compile and fix code in a loop many times per task

I measured big gains in both speed and memory against kotlinc 2.4.21, running warm as in the Gradle daemon:

- kotlinx-coroutines-core: 2.50 s → 159 ms (16x)

- Ktor core modules: 2.32 s → 226 ms (10x)

- kotlinpoet: 1.23 s → 97 ms (13x)

- Memory: ~1 GB → ~100 MB

What it doesn't do yet:

- A few language features aren't supported

- No warnings, and only the errors that type checking finds, so some invalid code compiles

- JVM only, no Gradle plugin or IDE support

- Passes 95% of kotlinc's box tests

It's a prototype, but I plan to keep working on it until it's useful for a wide range of real projects.

Benchmark details and how to repeat them: https://github.com/barteo/kotlin-compiler-go/blob/main/docs/...

comment_text.value:
> the system worked

Not really! There were several systemic failures:

1. It happened due to forecasting errors. Nothing remarkable happened that day, there were no sudden station trips or natural disasters. The margin was gone mostly due to planned maintenances combined with incorrectly forecasting demand. Whether the root cause is decentralized PV or not, the core issue is that the lowest frequency ever recorded happened on a totally unremarkable day. That can't be said to be the system working correctly.

2. The UK had to suddenly cut exports that had already been agreed and paid for, outside of normal systems. That puts it in a bad situation in future where allies may now do the same in reverse. A sudden unannounced cut in exports can be absorbed by the European grid but might not be absorbed by the British grid, which is smaller.

3. There were no EMNs issued and in the aftermath whistleblowers inside NESO claimed control room staff had been forbidden from taking notes or letting people know what happened. Information about this came out via newspaper articles in a drip drip months after the event. We're talking about this now and not in June because of this. That lack of transparency can't be said to be the system working.

4. The French were able to ship power hundreds of kilometers across France and under the sea to the south of England, but the UK couldn't move power the much smaller difference from its own north to south. That's another form of planning failure.

> Removing solar isn't helpful (that would just move the problem to earlier in the day.)

That depends what you think the problem is. The root of the event was forecasting errors, and the root of those come from the apparent difficulty of predicting how decentralized solar behaves especially at a sub-region level. Removing solar, or simply having never built it at all, actually would fix that problem.

All of this was predicted decades ago by conservatives so it's no good to just despair that they will "make hay" from being right (nobody will benefit from a big UK blackout, it will be bad news for everyone). They warned repeatedly that putting too much solar/wind into the grid will destabilize it and create huge price increases. Both of those warnings have come true in Europe. Solar/wind aren't reliable and so need thermal/hydro that's staffed, warmed up and ready to spin at a moment's notice but government policy ignores this and the stresses are now showing - both engineering and political (the apparent need for whistleblowers shows this).

N.B. the root cause of the Iberian blackout was a solar farm malfunctioning and desynchronizing from the grid, and when the control room tried to bring gas generation back online to stabilize things they couldn't do it fast enough because the plant was cold. It had been taken offline in the morning to make way for solar.

These problems don't really need extremely powerful hardware, and extremely large and expensive frontier AI agent swarms. comment_text.value:
My layman's understanding is that these models are very capable pattern matchers. When they need to do X, they go on a hunt for every pattern they could find and try to satisfy solving X. If that is not deemed good enough? make them dig harder and they take a different route to find patterns to solve X. Now, their arsenal is everything that they have been trained on(which is a lot!). This ability comes in extremely handy to apply existing techniques and patterns in ways we humans didn't quite think of.. because we are domain driven. A mathematical model about finding a good enough approximation of something at much lower cost is perhaps well understood in its applications in mathematics or whoever got to see those results. But, these LLMs, when pushed harder and harder might bring that to apply and solve an entirely different problem like for example, classifying whether some event is fraudulent. When it does such things, it _feels_ novel because it ended up using something we haven't thought of yet. But, it got there by brute force, stroke of luck, or some random path. I guess this is the reason why the frontier labs run those crazy swarms of AI agents to uncover all such paths turn them into chartered thinking vectors instead of random attempts.

I like to believe we humans still retain the ability to think completely outside the box and discover new phenomena and understanding aided by these pattern machines. In other words, these models are great at running combinations through patterns and we humans go one level higher and add those new patterns for them to accelerate us even more. We determine what to solve and the LLMs help us solve it faster.

I've been saying the same thing, Aaron Swartz arguably contributed more meaningful things long before AI, and was basically forced to make one of the worst decisions a person can make (at least in my opinion).

If you're unaware of who he was, or what happened to him:

* He was one of 12 others who helped to spec out RSS' standard (when he was 14 years old).

* He is widely considered a co-founder of reddit, after merging with reddit, he rewrote the majority of its codebase from Lisp to Python.

* He was one of the reasons Reddit protested SOPA back in the day (the same day that good 'old Kim Dotcom was raided and arrested by the US, the irony of which being that they swore up and down that they needed SOPA in order to do what they did to Kim Dotcom).

* I didn't know this before: he also developed the markdown publishing format with John Gruber.

What happened to him?

He was charged with felonies for stealing PDFs for publicly funded research papers, he was tried as if he hacked these systems. He took his own life as a result of them throwing decades of prison time at him for what's hardly a serious hacking offense (seriously, Kevin Mitnick was way worse). Kevin Mitnick served five years, they were looking to throw up to 35 years at him, and a minimum sentence of seven years if he went to trial.

It is abhorrent to me that we have people doing more malicious hacks that get no repercussions. Someone at OpenAI / Anthropic should be 100% liable for criminal charges of what their AI models do. Need I remind everyone, that these models can run way faster than what we common folk can see, the speed at which they run these models internally can go so quickly that by the time the model is discovered to have hacked someone, it could very well be too late. Just try the "fast" feature of Claude Code, now imagine Claude launching thousands of sub-agents at top speed internally, the capacity for unprecedented destruction is the most concerning thing to me, I say that as someone who uses Claude every week.

comment_text.value:
Math is an interesting case. Arguably a lot of the groundwork was already there. There’s a huge body of academic literature that’s historically been difficult for humans to draw on for various reasons. It’s relatively easier for LLMs to mine all of that for relevant prior work that it can recycle into proof segments to try. And we have theorem proving software that it can use to try out these proof segments and validate them. That creates a tight, self-contained, and relatively inexpensive feedback loop that lends itself well to a host of agents grinding away, as long as you have budget to pay for all that LLM inference.

I’m not sure the same conditions exist in other fields that deal with real world phenomena. Experiments to test hypotheses about biology or physics can take years and cost millions of dollars to run. They rarely scale down to the millipennies and milliseconds scale that makes letting a swarm of agents throw a bunch of shit at the wall and see what sticks a feasible option for finding mathematical proofs.

I don't see how you get to the conclusion that the original commenter thinks people are being gullible.

I look at the original comment and it doesn't say anything about gullibility. It expresses frustration that there's an influx of people interested in the field of Reverse Engineering but aren't digging deeper to where the answers are. I read the comment as being more similar to the complaints of the Eternal September, when an existing culture got permanently swamped by people who wanted to interact with the tools of the culture but didn't realise there was a process to learn first.

For myself, I'm glad there's an influx of people interested in technology and being able to grasp at the tools that can deliver outcomes. I don't love seeing people appearing that want to tell me that deeper understanding is dead, not because it does me any particular daily harm but because I think there's still a lot of value in understanding the details of a topic which summaries tend to gloss over. I've been feeling this for a long time, though, it's not related to LLMs but to a culture of knowledge more fixated on soundbites than on getting at the truth of things.

In this case, I see the original commenter reflecting my own concerns, but that's so often the way: we see things as we are, not as they are, which may be colouring my read.

Reasonable minds can disagree, of course, and I respect that we may just be reading the comment quite differently.
